::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a fingerprint, not the finger"}
A border control system doesn't keep your finger. It keeps a fingerprint: something derived from you that can be checked against you, but from which nobody can rebuild your hand.

A **password hash** is the password's fingerprint. Atlas stores the hash, and at login it hashes what you typed and compares. If the database is ever stolen, the thieves have fingerprints, not passwords. This lesson's job is to make turning a fingerprint back into a password so slow that it isn't worth trying.
:::

## The problem

Atlas needs accounts: saved issues and notes belong to someone. The oldest way to sign in is an email and a password, so Atlas must store something that lets it check a password later.

The one rule that matters most: **assume the database will leak.** Databases leak through SQL injection (lesson 3.8), a misconfigured backup, a stolen laptop with a copy, a former employee. And people reuse passwords, so a leaked password list unlocks their email, their bank and their GitHub account too. What you store must be useless, or at least very expensive, to whoever steals it.

Storing the password itself is plainly wrong. Less obviously, so is storing a quick hash of it. The "Attack it" section below shows why with a real experiment; the theory first.

## Theory

### Hash functions

A **hash function** turns any input into a fixed-size output, and can't be run backwards. You met SHA-256 in lesson 2.3 (TLS uses it). The same input always gives the same output, so checking a password means hashing what was typed and comparing.

"Can't be run backwards" is not the same as "can't be guessed". An attacker with a stolen hash simply hashes guesses until one matches. Two properties decide how long that takes:

- **Speed.** A fast hash lets the attacker try more guesses per second. For checking file integrity, speed is good; for passwords, slowness is the protection.
- **Salt.** If two people choose the same password, a plain hash gives the same output, and the attacker can hash each guess *once* and check it against every user at the same time. A **salt** is a random value generated for each password and stored with its hash, so equal passwords produce different hashes, and every user must be attacked separately.

### Password hashing functions

A **password hashing function** is salted, slow on purpose and **memory-hard**: each hash needs a block of memory as well as time, which takes away most of the advantage of graphics cards (GPUs) and custom chips, whose many small cores have little memory each. **Argon2** won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition and is the first recommendation of the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (OWASP is a widely referenced non-profit for web security).

Argon2 output carries everything needed to check it later:

```text
>>> hash_password("correct-horse-battery")
'$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$jlJFr+xvCWogMi+kkwzSyQ$NH69yowiHAeac31TEyg2NNO4fF5XWdPoWWixHBC3o+U'
>>> hash_password("correct-horse-battery")
'$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$neWWuFzoDo5TKWRatStQuw$Ef12E5mb0eENsw35eshL6wviUrLxYyKrffFSAC2lBLc'
```

Same password, different hashes, because each has a fresh salt. Reading the first one: algorithm `argon2id`, version 19, 64 MiB of memory (`m=65536` kibibytes), 3 passes over it (`t=3`), 4 lanes in parallel (`p=4`), then the salt, then the hash itself.

### Two ways the login form can leak

1. **Different messages**: "no such email" for one address and "wrong password" for another tells an attacker which emails are registered. That list is valuable on its own: for targeted phishing, or for trying passwords leaked from other sites.
2. **Different timing**: even with identical messages, if an unknown email returns at once while a real one waits for the hash, a stopwatch tells them apart. "Attack it" measures this too.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  R[register: email + password] --> H[Argon2 hash with a new salt]
  H --> DB[(users.password_hash)]
  L[login: email + password] --> F{user found?}
  F -->|no| D[hash a dummy anyway] --> X[401 Incorrect email or password]
  F -->|yes| V{verify password<br/>against stored hash}
  V -->|no| X
  V -->|yes| T[issue tokens, lesson 4.8]
```

## Attack it: crack a leaked table

The experiment: 1,000 leaked accounts whose owners picked predictable passwords, a word plus a number (`dragon42`, `summer7`). The attacker's guess list holds all 10,000 such combinations. Real attackers' lists hold billions of passwords leaked from earlier breaches, so this is a small, fair version of a real attack. The full script is about 60 lines; its three parts:

```python
# 1. Unsalted SHA-256: hash every guess once, then look each user up.
lookup = {sha256(guess): guess for guess in GUESSES}
cracked = sum(1 for stored in table if stored in lookup)

# 2. Salted SHA-256: every user needs their own pass over the guess list.
for salt, stored in salted:
    if any(sha256(salt + guess) == stored for guess in GUESSES):
        cracked += 1

# 3. Argon2 (salted, slow on purpose): measure, then work out what the full attack would take.
for guess in GUESSES[:20]:
    hasher.verify(guess, stored)
```

On one ordinary laptop core:

```text
1000 leaked accounts; the attacker's guess list has 10,000 entries
unsalted SHA-256: cracked 1000/1000 in 0.006s
salted SHA-256:   cracked 1000/1000 in 2.3s
Argon2:           52 ms per guess -> one user 9 min, all 1000 users 6 days
```

Read it carefully:

- **Unsalted SHA-256** fell in six thousandths of a second: one pass over the guess list cracked everyone.
- **Salt** forced a separate attack per user, and still every account fell in about two seconds, because SHA-256 is fast. On a graphics card, which computes billions of SHA-256 hashes a second, even a billion-entry guess list is cheap.
- **Argon2** with pwdlib's recommended settings costs 52 ms per guess. Trying this small list against every user takes about six days of computer time, and a real list of a billion guesses would take about a year and a half per user, for each of the 1,000 users. Its memory-hardness keeps graphics cards from closing most of that gap.

(The Argon2 figures are worked out from 20 measured guesses, since running the full attack would take six days. The worst case is shown; on average, a password is found halfway through the list.)

The lesson: **salt stops attacks at scale; slowness makes each guess expensive. You need both, and a password hashing function gives you both.** Nothing helps a user whose password is `password1`, which is why Atlas requires at least 10 characters (lesson 4.3), and why lesson 4.9 adds signing in with GitHub, which has no password stored at Atlas at all.

## Attack it: who has an account?

The login route gives one message for every failure. Now the stopwatch: 30 failed logins for a registered email and 30 for an unknown one, against the real API, median times:

```text
== without the dummy hash
registered email, wrong password: 53.1 ms
unknown email:                    3.4 ms
```

A fifteen-fold difference, visible across the internet. Anyone can test a list of addresses and learn which are registered. The defence: when the email is unknown, hash *something* anyway, so both paths do the same expensive work:

```text
== with the dummy hash
registered email, wrong password: 54.7 ms
unknown email:                    52.5 ms
```

The remaining difference is smaller than the normal variation between runs.

## In the project

### Red: what "stored safely" means

Lesson 4.5's rule: the test first. In `tests/test_api_auth.py`:

```python
def test_register_never_returns_the_password(client: TestClient) -> None:
    response = client.post(
        "/auth/register", json={"email": "Ada@Example.com", "password": "a-long-password"}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    body = response.json()
    assert body["email"] == "ada@example.com"
    assert body["role"] == "user"
    assert "password" not in body and "password_hash" not in body


def test_passwords_are_stored_as_argon2_hashes(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    sign_up(client, "ada@example.com")

    stored = session.scalar(select(User.password_hash).where(User.email == "ada@example.com"))
    assert stored is not None and stored.startswith("$argon2")
```

`sign_up` is a small helper in `conftest.py` that registers and logs in through the API. The second test reads the database directly, through the same rolled-back `session` the routes use, because the rule is about what's *stored*, which no API response shows.

Here is that test catching a tempting mistake, a `hash_password` written with `hashlib.sha256`:

```text
E       AssertionError: assert ('05659b9c139ca08da5dab519fa526d6286fd71104a1d763a7acd945ce42b4957' is not None and False)
E        +  where False = <built-in method startswith of str object at 0x7fe1dd169300>('$argon2')
FAILED tests/test_api_auth.py::test_passwords_are_stored_as_argon2_hashes - A...
1 failed, 1 passed, 15 deselected in 0.26s
```

### Green: hashing with pwdlib

```bash
uv add "pwdlib[argon2]"
```

**pwdlib** is a small, maintained password hashing library (by the author of FastAPI Users) with Argon2 as its recommended default. `src/atlas/security.py`:

```python
from pwdlib import PasswordHash

# Argon2 is deliberately slow and memory-hungry, so guessing passwords from a
# leaked hash is expensive. Never use a fast hash like SHA-256 for passwords.
_password_hasher = PasswordHash.recommended()


def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return _password_hasher.hash(password)


def verify_password(password: str, password_hash: str) -> bool:
    return _password_hasher.verify(password, password_hash)
```

`security.py` imports nothing from FastAPI (lesson 4.6), so `atlas make-admin` and the tests can use it too.

### The `User` table

In `models.py` (the key parts):

```python
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    __table_args__ = (
        CheckConstraint("role IN ('user', 'admin')", name="users_role_valid"),
        # Every account signs in somehow: with an email and password, or with GitHub.
        CheckConstraint(
            "password_hash IS NOT NULL OR github_id IS NOT NULL", name="users_can_sign_in"
        ),
    )

    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(320), unique=True)
    # Never the password itself: an Argon2 hash (lesson 4.7).
    password_hash: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(200))
    github_id: Mapped[int | None] = mapped_column(BigInteger, unique=True)
    github_login: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(100))
    role: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(10), default="user", server_default="user")
    skills_profile: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(Text, default="", server_default="")
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(DateTime(timezone=True), server_default=func.now())
```

`email` and `password_hash` may be empty because lesson 4.9 adds accounts that sign in with GitHub only. The second check constraint (lesson 3.5) makes sure every account has *some* way to sign in.

### Registering

`routes/auth.py`:

```python
@router.post("/register", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=UserOut)
def register(body: UserCreate, session: SessionDep) -> User:
    user = User(email=body.email, password_hash=hash_password(body.password))
    session.add(user)
    try:
        session.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        # The unique constraint on email decides, so two simultaneous sign-ups can't both win.
        session.rollback()
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT, "An account with this email exists") from None
    session.refresh(user)
    return user
```

Why not check "does this email exist?" first, then insert? Two requests could both check, both see "no", and both insert: a race condition (lesson 3.7). The database's unique constraint is the one place that can decide reliably; the route turns its `IntegrityError` into **409 Conflict**. `HTTPException` is FastAPI's way to stop a route and answer with an error status.

```text
$ uv run pytest tests/test_api_auth.py -k "argon2 or never_returns" -q
2 passed, 15 deselected in 0.40s

$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "password": "correct-horse-battery"}'
{"id":3,"email":"ada@example.com","github_login":null,"role":"user","skills_profile":"","created_at":"2026-11-18T03:10:48.623999Z"}

$ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email": "ada@example.com", "password": "correct-horse-battery"}'
{"error":{"code":"conflict","message":"An account with this email exists","request_id":"bdf1ecf8ff914f2286efde548b515861"}}
```

Doesn't that 409 reveal that the email is registered? Yes. Registration can't avoid it without email confirmation (sending "you already have an account" to the address instead of answering on screen), which Atlas doesn't do. Login, where guessing is cheap and repeated, is where the uniform answer matters most.

### Checking a password, with the timing defence

Lesson 4.8 turns this into a full login. The checking part:

```python
TIMING_DUMMY_HASH = hash_password("not-a-real-password")

if user is None or user.password_hash is None:
    # Hash anyway, so an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password:
    # otherwise response times would reveal which emails have accounts.
    verify_password(form.password, TIMING_DUMMY_HASH)
    raise wrong_credentials
if not verify_password(form.password, user.password_hash):
    raise wrong_credentials
```

A test that measured response times would fail at random on a busy computer, so the reference suite guards the defence another way: it counts how many hashes each failed login performs, and expects one for a real account *and* one for an unknown email.

```python
async def test_unknown_emails_cost_one_hash_like_real_ones(
    client: httpx.AsyncClient, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch
) -> None:
    """Guards against the timing attack in lesson 4.7 without measuring time (which is flaky)."""
    await sign_up(client, "ada@example.com")
    hashed: list[str] = []

    def counting_verify(password: str, password_hash: str) -> bool:
        hashed.append(password_hash)
        return security.verify_password(password, password_hash)

    monkeypatch.setattr(auth, "verify_password", counting_verify)

    for email in ("ada@example.com", "nobody@example.com"):
        await client.post("/auth/login", data={"username": email, "password": "wrong-password"})

    assert len(hashed) == 2
```

(It's written in the async style of lesson 4.17, where the reference code ends up; the idea is the same.) `monkeypatch.setattr` swaps the route module's `verify_password` for one that counts its calls. With the dummy hash removed, it fails exactly as it should:

```text
E       AssertionError: assert 1 == 2
```

## Trade-offs: choosing a password hash *(deep dive)*

| Algorithm | Salted | Slow | Memory-hard | Where you'll meet it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 alone | no (unless added) | no | no | Old systems; never for passwords |
| PBKDF2 | yes | yes, by repeating a fast hash many times | no | Standards-driven environments; Django's default |
| bcrypt | yes | yes | a little | Very widely deployed; fine to keep; limits passwords to 72 bytes |
| scrypt | yes | yes | yes | Some systems and cryptocurrencies |
| **Argon2id** | yes | yes | yes | Current first recommendation; Atlas |

If you inherit a system with bcrypt or PBKDF2, you don't need an emergency migration: re-hash each password with Argon2 the next time its owner logs in (the only moment you have the plain password). pwdlib can verify several algorithms and tell you when a hash needs upgrading.

## Common mistakes

- **Storing passwords, or encrypting them.** Encryption can be reversed by whoever holds the key; hashing can't.
- **Using SHA-256 or MD5 for passwords**, even with a salt: the experiment above cracked every account in two seconds.
- **Writing your own hashing scheme.** Use a maintained library with Argon2.
- **Different messages, or different timing,** for "unknown email" and "wrong password".
- **Logging request bodies** on the login route: the password ends up in your logs (lesson 4.15).
- **No upper limit on password length**: a megabyte "password" makes the server hash a megabyte (lesson 4.3).

## Check yourself

**1.** In the experiment, salted SHA-256 still fell in seconds. What did the salt achieve, then?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It stopped the attacker from hashing each guess once and checking all 1,000 users at the same time: each user needed their own pass over the guess list, 1,000 times the work. That matters at scale, but SHA-256 is so fast that 1,000 times "almost nothing" is still very little. Salt and slowness solve different halves of the problem.
:::

**2.** Why does Atlas hash a dummy value when the email is unknown?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
So an unknown email takes as long to reject as a wrong password for a real account. Without it, unknown emails answered in about 3 ms and real ones in about 53 ms, so anyone could learn which emails are registered by timing the responses.
:::

**3.** Why does registration rely on the unique constraint instead of checking first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Check-then-insert is a race: two simultaneous requests can both pass the check. The database enforces uniqueness atomically, so exactly one insert wins and the other gets an `IntegrityError`, which becomes 409.
:::

## Exercise

Write a test, red first, that a password of 129 characters is rejected at registration with 422, and that no user row is created. (It should pass straight away, because lesson 4.3's `Password` type already limits length. Make it fail first by temporarily raising the limit, to prove it tests something.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
def test_overlong_passwords_are_rejected(client: TestClient, session: Session) -> None:
    response = client.post(
        "/auth/register", json={"email": "ada@example.com", "password": "x" * 129}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 422
    assert session.scalar(select(User).where(User.email == "ada@example.com")) is None
```
With `max_length=1000` in `Password`, the request succeeds with 201 and both asserts fail; with 128 it passes. Changing the code to see a test fail, then changing it back, is a quick way to check a test that passed on its first run. Not in the reference code.
:::

## Stretch

Run the cracking experiment yourself with `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password, salt, 600_000)` as a fourth method (600,000 rounds is a commonly recommended setting for PBKDF2 with SHA-256). Measure its time per guess and compare with Argon2. What does PBKDF2 lack that Argon2 has?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Time a few guesses as the script does for Argon2. On the machine used for this course, one PBKDF2 guess took about 106 ms: on a single CPU core it's as slow as Argon2, or slower. What it lacks is memory-hardness: each guess needs almost no memory, so a graphics card can run thousands of guesses side by side and recover most of the speed the attacker lost. Argon2's 64 MiB per guess prevents that.
:::

`security.py` gains `hash_password` and `verify_password`; `models.py` gains `User`; `routes/auth.py` gains `POST /auth/register`; tests for storage and the timing defence. `pwdlib[argon2]` added.
